For most of my life, I've struggled with my weight. Due to a mix of ADHD and a metabolism that seems to be constantly in overdrive, I've been underweight for practically my entire childhood. Combined with medications for said ADHD, which are notorious for appetite killing, I struggled to even breach 100 lb; I was 12, 5'6" and 75 lb before I flat out refused to take anymore medications on account of my weight, and I ended up gaining 60 pounds in 2 months following. However, in the next 8 years I was never able to gain any significant amount of weight in a short time. Slowly I crept up and ended hovering around 155-160 lb, rail thin for being 6'2"; if I had a shirt off, all of my ribs were visible from a distance. The frustrating part was that in order to maintain that weight I was eating 4 full meals a day, 3 would see my weight slowly drop.

Anyways, following the breakup with my ex fiance, I dropped down to 130 lb in the subsequent depression from a lack of eating enough. After I started to recover from that, I swore to myself that as soon as I had the funds, I'd throw myself fully into the gym and work so I'd no longer be embarrassed to take off my shirt, etc. I prepped a workout regiment, meal regiment, and which supplements to take. Last June I started a great summer job and finally got to start working out. From June to January, I managed to go from 150 lb to 195 lb, was in the gym 3 hours a day, 6 days a week, eating 5-6 meals each day. I was in fantastic shape and was loving every bit of it. Then mid January, I injured my rotator cuff, and later in early March I broke my foot while running. This week I got an MRI on my shoulder as it's been still giving my problems after 6 months of Physical Therapy, and I'm hoping like crazy that it's not a tear. So for the past several months, I've been unable to do any form of work out, and it's been driving me fucking crazy. All the while, I've lost 30 pounds as I've curbed my eating habits due to being fairly inactive for months (only 4 meals a day right now).

And the infuriating part is seeing and hearing fat people complain about being overweight and not being able to lose the pounds. It's not fucking hard. All it takes is a little dedication to not eating like shit, and getting a bit active. You fat fucks are choosing to be that way. You are fucking choosing to be lazy globs of pustular excrement. Every day I get to look at the protein powder and supplements sitting collecting dust as I wait for this fucking injury to heal, hopefully without having to get surgery and take another 6 months of waiting. But no, the glutenous pigs would rather choose to be lazy when they could fix themselves easily.

TL;DR: Hard for me to gain weight, but finally ended up going to the gym last summer and gained weight and muscle. Got injured in January & March, angry at being unable to workout while hams choose to be lazy fucks.

I'm married and never told my wife, but I told her earlier this year. I was feeling incredibly "unwell" by not being honest with her about it. I had tried really hard to tell her several times but chickened out. After we got married I felt a building pressure to tell her. The arguments in my head were “what is the point, I'm committed to monogamy” vs. “she doesn’t actually know who I am deep down”.

It lead me to feel pretty unconfident and just altogether ‘wrong’. She eventually got it out of me one night, after I had spent that day warring between telling her and not. I had chickened out again and we were going to bed but she could tell how distraught I was about something and with enough gentle pressure got me to tell her. My wording was “honey I have never told anyone this, but I have never considered myself 100% straight. I very much prefer women, but I know I’m not straight”. Her reaction straight away was to kind of nod and get teared up and hug me. She then complained how unfair it was that society made it so hard for us to be ourselves etc. I think she was trying to find something to say at that point but I was just so relieved she didn’t run a mile. We chatted a bit about how it was for me when I was growing up etc. and I was feeling incredibly relieved and peaceful.

Her reaction 2 days later was a bit more what I had been expecting. This was when she cried a little bit and asked for more detail, why had I never told her this, what did I expect her to do with this information etc. She wasn’t ‘unaccepting me’ but I think she was just trying to figure out what the hell I’d just told her and what it meant (quite rightly). We chatted about it and I spent some time apologising for the deceit. I also spent a lot of time reassuring her how much I wanted her and that I had made the choice a long time ago that she was for me. I knew that her reaction was going to come at some point and she deserved the answers. I still don’t regret telling her for a second, best thing she ever made me do lol. These days we don’t really discuss it much, the odd comment now and then but it’s pretty much just added to part of who I am.

I came out separately to different people in my life, and each one was a different experience.

The first person I came out to was my best friend, Natalie. We were just talking and our conversation eventually turned to personal stuff. She told me a secret of hers (which, of course, I won't be sharing), and I told her about my bisexuality. She was very supportive of me, and happy that I was finally beginning to come out. She also said that she was not at all surprised, and was wondering if/when I was going to tell her.

The next person I told was my dad, which was several years later. We were in the car on the way to go hunting, which we've been doing every deer season since I was very young. I don't remember what we were talking about beforehand, but I just sort of... blurted it out to him. I was not planning on it, it just sort of happened. He was really awkward about it and asked a lot of weird, somewhat invasive questions, but--surprisingly--he was not outwardly negative about my "confession". Like with Natalie, he also said that he was not surprised, and had suspected that I was not straight for a long while. I think he was relieved that I wasn't a "full lesbian" more than he was upset that I was bisexual.
He did, however, say that I had to tell my mother within a week of us returning home, or that he would tell her for me.

I have struggled with an anxiety disorder my whole life, so that sort of pressure was not very helpful. The last day of my dad's "deadline", I sat with my mom at the kitchen table. I tried to find a way to bring up the topic and tell her about my sexuality, but... well... I ended up just sitting in silence for a couple minutes and then just randomly bursting into tears. She managed to get enough information out of me through my crying to put things together on her own, and immediately made sure that I knew that she loved and supported me. Like both Natalie and my dad, she also said that she had seen something like this coming.

Now, despite both of my parents seeming to be okay with my sexuality, they really weren't that comfortable with it. They are both conservative/religious types, and have never been shy about speaking their mind on how they felt about non-straight-ness. I know that they both thought--and almost certainly still think--that having feelings for those of the same sex is a sign of severe mental illness, and neither are particularly happy about the recent supreme court ruling that happened in late June. They both are not comfortable talking about it, and I'm pretty sure that they are disappointed in the fact that I didn't turn out to be the "good little straight religious girl" that they wanted me to be. But, luckily, they keep their mouths shut. For the most part.

After them, the next person that I came out to was my boyfriend at the time. He was going through a lot of trouble in his own home, and admitted to me that he was struggling with some mental health problems, as well as the fact that he felt vulnerable and uncomfortable with telling me such a big secret of his. I told him about my sexuality in order to help him relax, which worked pretty well and got him to calm down and feel more confident in himself. Unfortunately, he later told me that he was not happy with my sexuality, and he frequently used it to shame me in many ways. He ended up being quite abusive to me in many ways, and he used the fact that I was bisexual to manipulate our relationship and make himself into a victim and make me into some sort of villain.

The final person that I truly came out to was my sister. I've always been very close to her, and it was eating me up inside that she was the only immediate family member that I hadn't told. I tried to find the best possible time to bring it up with her, but--as many of you probably know--it's not all that easy to find the "perfect moment". Eventually, I just went into her room one day and told her outright that I was bisexual. She seemed mildly surprised at the sudden-ness of the statement, but was overall very chill about it. I still remember her response to me: "That's nice. Tell me something I don't know."

After her, I never really "came out" to anyone else. I don't consider myself in the closet anymore. If it comes up, I don't hide it from people. I didn't post a status update, but my Facebook profile says that I'm interested in both males and females. It's caused some problems with certain people, but most of the time it's not an issue.

I guess that's my "coming out story", then. Sorry if it's too ramble-y.
